ABSTRACT 
Background. The association between psoriasis and some diseases has become relevant in recent 
years. Providing appropriate management of psoriasis from an early stage requires prompt diagnosis 
and treatment of concomitant diseases and to prevent any potential comorbidity. This approach 
should consider the adverse events of the drugs used to treat psoriasis potentially related to the 
onset of comorbidities. 
 
Objective. To provide the dermatologist with an accurate and friendly tool for systematising the 
diagnosis of psoriasis-associated comorbidities, which generally escapes the scope of the 
dermatology setting, and to facilitate decision-making about the referral and treatment of patients 
with comorbidities. 
 
Methods. These position statement recommendations were developed by a working group 
composed of ten experts (four dermatologists, one cardiologist, one rheumatologist, one 
gastroenterologist, one nephrologist, one endocrinologist, and one psychiatrist) and two health 
services researchers. The expert group selected the psoriasis comorbidities considered according to 
their relevance in the dermatology setting. The recommendations on diagnostic criteria are based on 
the current clinical practice guidelines for each of the comorbidities. The information regarding the 
repercussion of psoriasis medical treatments on associated comorbid diseases was obtained from 
the summary of product characteristics of each drug.

Results. Recommendations were developed to detect and refer the following psoriasis 
comorbidities: Psoriatic arthritis, cardiovascular risk factors (diabetes, dyslipidaemia, obesity, 
hypertension, and metabolic syndrome), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, inflammatory bowel 
disease, kidney disease, and psychological disorders (anxiety and depression). In addition, alcohol 
and tobacco consumption were included. The tables and figures are precise, easy-to-use tools to 
systematise the diagnosis of comorbidities in patients with psoriasis and facilitate the decision-
making process regarding referral and treatment of patients with an associated disease. 
 
Conclusion. The application of these position statement recommendations will facilitate the 
dermatologist practice, and benefit psoriasis patients’ health and quality of life. 
 
INTRODUCTION 
Psoriasis is a skin disorder, with a prevalence in adults ranging from 0.91% to 8.5%1, usually 
associated with physical and psychological burden. Such burden is additionally increased by 
comorbid diseases that have been increasingly described as associated with psoriasis since 1897, 
when Strauss reported an association between psoriasis and diabetes2. These comorbidities include: 
Psoriatic arthritis (PsA), cardiovascular disease (CVD), cardiovascular risk factors (CVRF) including 
diabetes mellitus (DM), dyslipidaemia (DL), obesity (OB), hypertension (HT) and metabolic syndrome 
(MS), aortic valve stenosis, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease 
(NAFLD), kidney disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), sleep apnoea, peripheral 
vascular disease, autoimmune hepatitis, uveitis, periodontitis, atrial fibrillation, sexual dysfunction, 
multiple sclerosis, osteoporosis, anxiety, depression, and tumours, especially lymphoma, and even 
tobacco and alcohol consumption .3-26 In addition, psoriasis is usually treated with drugs that may 
interfere with some comorbidities, mainly through their adverse effects.25,27 Therefore, to address a 
comprehensive management of psoriasis and its comorbidities, it is critical to establish the 
dermatologist’s role in the diagnosis of psoriasis comorbidities and the criteria for referral to the 
appropriate specialist. 
 
Several guidelines, consensus, or recommendations have addressed the psoriasis comorbidities issue 
with different approaches and perspectives in recent years.3-5,25,26 Based on the clinical practice 
guideline for an integrated approach to comorbidity in patients with psoriasis published by Daudén 
et al,25,26 we developed the present position statement, including a new comorbidity (kidney disease) 
and updating recommendations on referral criteria according to the most recent guidelines specific 
for each comorbidity. In addition, given the important role of the general practitioner (GP) in health 
care systems, we specify which type of patients should be referred to the GP or to the appropriate 
specialist. This position statement focuses on the comorbidities most frequently cited as associated 
with psoriasis and relevant for the dermatologist at the clinical setting (PsA, CVRF, NAFLD, IBD, 
kidney disease, anxiety, depression, tobacco and alcohol consumption). In addition, it summarizes 
the effects of psoriasis medical treatments on comorbidities. 
 
The objective of these position statement recommendations is to provide the dermatologist with an 
accurate and friendly tool for systematizing the diagnosis of comorbidities, which generally escapes 
the scope of this speciality, and to facilitate decision-making about the referral and treatment of 
patient with psoriasis-associated comorbidities.

MATERIALS AND METHODS 
The recommendations of this position statement were developed by a working group composed of 
ten experts (four dermatologists, one cardiologist, one rheumatologist, one gastroenterologist, one 
nephrologist, one endocrinologist, and one psychiatrist) and two health services researchers. The 
expert group selected the following comorbidities to be considered in these recommendations: PsA, 
CVRF (DM, DL, OB, HT and MS), NAFLD, IBD, kidney disease, anxiety, depression, and tobacco and 
alcohol consumption. These comorbidities were selected because of their high prevalence among 
psoriasis patients confirmed consistently in several studies, and their clinical relevance in psoriasis. 
 
The scientific evidence on the association of these comorbidities with psoriasis, except for kidney 
disease, was reviewed in previous publications.25,26 For this reason, only the evidence of the 
association between psoriasis and kidney disease was reviewed for the present work. We performed 
a PubMed search for articles on kidney disease prevalence in psoriasis, published in English or 
Spanish from April 29, 2010 to December 31, 2017. Search terms used were “Psoriasis” and “Renal 
or Kidney” and “Prevalence or Risk, or Frequency”. Two reviewers (PLM and AJBB) screened titles 
and abstracts of the retrieved articles, and data on prevalence, incidence and impact on mortality 
were summarised. In addition, the review of publications on comorbidities studied in the previous 
guideline25,26 was updated until December 30, 2017. This review confirms the evidence of psoriasis 
association with each of the comorbidities studied.3-20 
 
Recommendations on diagnostic criteria were based on the most recent clinical practice guidelines 
(CPG) for each comorbidity and their corresponding screening tests. Screening tests for alcohol 
dependence and anxiety/depression were selected based on user-friendliness, wide availability, and 
current use. Recommendations on oriented medical histories and additional testing were proposed 
by the expert group based on the guidelines for diagnostic criteria found in the clinical practice 
guidelines reviewed. Criteria regarding referrals were made by consensus using the best scientific 
evidence available. 
 
In addition, we describe the effects of the psoriasis medical treatments on each of the comorbidities 
studied. We reviewed the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) of the drugs routinely used in 
psoriasis management. We included the following drugs: Ciclosporin, adalimumab, etanercept, 
infliximab, ustekinumab, secukinumab, ixekizumab, apremilast, acitretin, methotrexate, and 
dimethyl fumarate. The SmPCs were obtained from the Online Drug Information Centre of the 
Spanish Agency for Medicines and Health Products28. We considered only adverse reactions that are 
very frequent (≥1/10), frequent (between ≥1/100 and <1/10) or of unknown frequency, as well as 
the contraindications. 
 
To make these recommendations eminently practical and easy to use, the position statement 
content is presented in three structured tables: table 1 describes the association between psoriasis 
and kidney disease; table 2 presents the relevant aspects of clinical management in the 
dermatologist office; and table 3 shows the impact of the psoriasis medical treatments on each of 
the comorbidities studied.

RESULTS 
Prevalence of kidney disease in psoriasis and its degree of association 
The literature search performed to analyse information about the association between kidney 
disease and psoriasis found 47 hits of which 8 full texts were finally included. Figure 1 shows the 
PRISMA flow diagram.29 
 
The literature review provided data on incidence, prevalence, and mortality of kidney disease in 
psoriasis patients with several statistical measures of association. These measures of risk were often 
stratified by the severity of psoriasis and the severity of kidney disease and, in some studies, 
adjusted for age, gender and relevant patients’ characteristics including other comorbidities. Table 1 
summarises incidence, prevalence and mortality data of kidney disease, and the magnitude of their 
associations with psoriasis. 
 
Clinical recommendations for the management of comorbidities and referral criteria 
For each comorbidity or lifestyle habit, table 2 shows the issues to which the medical history should 
pay special attention, the specific physical examination required and the additional tests 
recommended. The goal of the medical history and physical examination is to reach a diagnostic 
approach to each patient’s clinical conditions, in our case, the psoriasis comorbidities. Annual 
medical history and physical examination are recommended for psoriasis patients with topical 
treatment, and every 6 months for patients on systemic treatment. 
 
Table 2 also presents criteria for referral to the appropriate specialist for patients with a new 
comorbidity diagnosed and for those previously diagnosed. For the latter, table 2 also guides the 
dermatologists regarding patient counselling and referral based on the clinical status and whether 
the disease is being properly managed by the specialist in charge. Figure 2 summarises data on table 
2 highlighting the key points for the clinical management of psoriasis comorbidities. 
 
Figure 3 summarises the tests and questionnaires recommended for the preliminary diagnosis and 
clinical follow-up of comorbidities in psoriasis. 
 
Impact of psoriasis medical treatment on comorbidities 
Table 3 describes the implications of psoriasis medical treatment on comorbidities. 
 
DISCUSSION 
Psoriasis is a disease associated with multiple comorbidities, which have been described in a variety 
of publications. In patients with psoriasis who suffer comorbidity the dermatologist should 
contribute to improve the treatment compliance and the appropriate follow-up, and to reinforce

recommendations on a healthy lifestyle, especially regarding tobacco and alcohol consumption, diet 
and exercise. A previous guideline, published in 2012,26 made specific recommendations on how to 
diagnose, when to refer patients to the appropriate specialist, and how to consider treatments in 
case of comorbidity. 
 
Given the aim of the present work, we included a new relevant psoriasis comorbidity (renal disease) 
and updated the recommendations for detecting potential comorbidities and referring the patient to 
the GP or the appropriate specialist. The group of experts established the level of referral (GP or 
specialist) thinking on the usual characteristics of most health care systems. However, the 
professional to whom the patient should be referred could be different depending on local 
circumstances, such as the centre conditions, the existence of specialised units, the continuity of 
care, the existence of multidisciplinary units, or even the personal relationship between the 
dermatologist and other specialists, among others. 
 
The first comorbidity studied in this position statement is PsA. Several instruments, such as the 
Psoriasis and Arthritis Questionnaire (PAQ)50, ToPAS,51 PASE52, and PEST53 have been developed to 
define and classify PsA. However, none of the questionnaires cited has achieved sufficient consensus 
to be universally accepted, and several of them have not been validated in many countries. The 
Classification Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis (CASPAR)38 is a tool that has gained acceptance for use in 
clinical practice. CASPAR criteria are simple, quick and easy to apply in clinical practice, but require 
radiological evidence of juxtaarticular new bone formation, which makes difficult its application 
outside a rheumatology practice. For the above reasons, we propose criteria for referral based on 
accepted definitions of inflammatory pain (peripheral or axial), enthesitis and dactylitis from a large 
international study38 and a report from the GRAPPA 2013 Annual Meeting.39 Consequently, patients 
meeting the criteria recommended in this guide should be referred with a suspicion of PsA, to be 
confirmed by the rheumatologist (Table 2). 
 
As in the previous guide, this position statement does not include diagnosis or treatment of CVD 
(myocardial infarction, angina, stroke, or peripheral vascular disease), despite the proved association 
between CVD and psoriasis found in the scientific literature.26 CVD-related diagnostic or referral 
criteria are not included in Table 2 because its diagnosis rarely takes place at a dermatology office. 
CVD symptoms are usually acute or severely disabling and, thus, promptly diagnosed and treated by 
the appropriate clinicians. Instead, in a dermatology setting, we consider more effective to provide 
recommendations for the identification of CVRF that may lead to the onset or progression of CVD. As 
psoriasis patients present a higher prevalence of CVRF than the general population, dermatologists 
are in a key position for early detection, management and appropriate referral of patients with 
CVRF. Early diagnosis of psoriasis comorbidities is important in all cases, but especially in those 
comorbidities whose progression may increase the risk of undesired consequences or even death. 
This is the case of CVRF. Therefore, the dermatologist should refer the patient to the appropriate 
specialist (e.g., cardiologist, endocrinologist, etc.) or to the general practitioner when a sign, 
symptom or test suggests a CVRF, as well as when the patient is a smoker (table 2).

One of the CVRF approached in this work is DL. Compared to the previous guideline,26 the present 
position statement does not consider high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-c) as a parameter to 
be considered for DL (table 2). Recent studies suggest that HDL-c is a complex molecule formed by 
several particles, which can be dysfunctional, thereby allowing high risk of atherosclerosis despite 
high HDL-c levels. Due to this fact and the lack of therapeutic options to increase its levels, our 
recommendations do not include this parameter as a refer-to-primary-care criterion. Besides, recent 
European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines of DL and cardiovascular prevention highlight LDL-c 
as the most important therapeutic target in DL.54 Therefore, the authors of the present position 
statement agree that the best strategy is to reduce LDL-c as much as possible in high risk patients. 
 
Another controversial issue is the definition of HT. In the present work, we considered to follow the 
recommendations of the 2016 ESC guidelines on cardiovascular prevention54 in which the threshold 
for the diagnosis of HT is 140/90 mmHg (table 2), although a recent American guideline55 lowered 
the highest normal range of BP to 130/80 mmHg. The latter cut-off might be useful for high or very 
high-risk patients, but for the general population it seems more reasonable to maintain the limit of 
140/90 mmHg or higher.56 Moreover, such a strict cut-off could lead to refer an excessive proportion 
of patients to primary care and also increase therapeutic inertia.57 
 
NAFLD is the most frequent liver disorder in western contries.58 Patients with psoriasis have higher 
prevalence of NAFLD, higher rate of severe disease, and worse prognosis.45 Suspicions concerning 
NAFLD should be present in the dermatology setting because many cases are asymptomatic. The 
pathogenic links between psoriasis and NAFLD are chronic inflammation and peripheral insulin 
resistance, which is a common finding in diseases associated with psoriasis. The dermatologist 
should be aware not only of the high prevalence of NAFLD in psoriasis but also of the presence of 
steatohepatitis (the inflammatory variant of fatty liver, at risk of developing liver fibrosis, cirrhosis 
and its complications), especially in case of severe psoriasis or MS. For this reason, the dermatologist 
should explore the presence of MS components (DM, OB, DL, and HT). Abnormal liver enzymes may 
be difficult to detect because elevations are usually mild. Liver enzymes can be normal in 15% to 
30% or more of patients with NAFLD, even though 35% of such patients have advanced fibrosis or 
cirrhosis.59 Given this situation, in the presence of key indicators of risk of NAFLD (components of 
Metabolic Syndrome) ultrasound imaging is indicated to rule out liver disease, even when 
biochemistry is normal.46 Once NAFLD has been confirmed, the dermatologist must cooperate in 
prescribing the necessary dietary measures and adjusting drug dosages, or even changing the 
treatment trying to avoid hepatotoxic drugs, if transaminase levels are elevated. The absence of liver 
damage according to the initial assessment does not exclude its development over the coming years. 
Therefore, patients will have to be reassessed if analyses reveal signs of damage or if MS develops.45 
 
Since the publication of the previous guideline,26 definitive scientific evidence on the association 
between kidney disease and psoriasis has been published30-37 (Table 1). Therefore, kidney disease is 
included as a new comorbidity in the present position statement. Several causes of kidney disease in 
patients with psoriasis have been reported: First, the kidney is a target organ of CVRF; second, 
autoimmune disorders can cause glomerular impairment; and third, some drugs used for psoriasis 
treatment are nephrotoxic.60 The association between impaired renal function, the onset of CVD, 
and death is well established.61 Since kidney disease could be asymptomatic in early stages, we 
recommend to determine albuminuria in a simple urine test, and serum creatinine, glomerular 
filtration rate (GFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) in all psoriasis patients (table 2).

According to the results of such tests and based on the KDIGO clinical practice guideline for the 
evaluation and management of chronic kidney disease,47 we recommend referring the patient to the 
GP if ACR ≥30 mg/g, and refer the patient to the nephrologist if ACR ≥300 mg/g or GFR<60 
ml/min/1.73 m2 (table 2). 
 
Regarding consumption habits, tobacco consumption should be detected by the dermatologist and 
considered not only as the main cause of COPD (comorbidity associated to psoriasis),11,62,63 but also 
as an important CVRF. For this reason, psoriasis patients should be advised to cease smoking to 
reduce their risk of COPD and CVD (table 2). In addition, about one-third of patients with moderate-
severe psoriasis have excessive alcohol consumption.64-66 This fact may contribute to the increase of 
mortality among psoriasis patients. A recent cohort study showed that people with psoriasis have 
approximately 60%greater risk of dying due to alcohol-related causes compared with peers of the 
same age and sex in the general population.67 Therefore, screening for alcohol abuse should be 
performed at the dermatologist office among patients diagnosed with psoriasis, using tests such as 
the CAGE questionnaire49,68 as we suggest in this position statement (table 2). 
 
Some diseases, such as IBD or PsA, should be diagnosed by a specialist; therefore, we consider 
sufficient for the dermatologist to perform an appropriate medical history and clinical examination 
and to refer the patient to the specialist without performing further diagnostic tests (table 2). 
 
Independently of the comorbidities discussed, dermatologists should be aware that many patients 
experience feelings of social rejection and stigmatisation because of their lesions, especially if these 
are visible. For these reasons, depression is a frequent comorbidity in patients with psoriasis26 and it 
is recommended that dermatologists explore the possible presence of depression using the HADS 
scale (table 2). Although some patients with depression have suicidal ideas, we do not recommend 
using any suicide questionnaire in the dermatology setting. We believe that with the HADS and the 
conversation at the clinic visit, the dermatologist may be able to suspect suicide ideas or severe 
depression that warrant referring the patient urgently to the psychiatrist. 
 
Finally, this document provides information on the adverse effects of the medication used for 
psoriasis treatment that can be considered as comorbidities (table 3). This will aid dermatologists in 
selecting the treatment that best fits the profile of each psoriasis patient, while also avoiding 
possible exacerbation of already existing comorbidities. 
 
In summary, the prevention of CVRF and the early diagnosis of PsA, renal disease, IBD, liver 
involvement, and depression and anxiety support the use of these position statement 
recommendations in dermatologic clinical practice. Its application will benefit the health and quality 
of life of psoriasis patients and prevent progression of comorbidities to more severe stages.
